## i18n-utils

### Roles and attributes

- The package exports no DOM parts; it is a thin layer over the `Intl` constructors with a shared memo cache. `i18nCache(Ctor)` keys instances by locale plus sorted option entries, so every formatter here is reused across calls and stale options never leak between locales. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/index.ts; zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/cache.ts)
- `formatBytes(bytes, locale = "en-US", options)` divides by 1000 (`unitSystem: "decimal"`, the default) or 1024 (`"binary"`), walks a prefix table (bits stop at tera, bytes continue to peta), applies `toPrecision(precision)` with a default precision of 3, and hands the result to `Intl.NumberFormat` with `style: "unit"` and the composed unit name such as `kilobyte` or `megabit`. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-bytes.ts)
- `formatList(list, locale, options)` delegates straight to `Intl.ListFormat`, so `type` (`conjunction`/`disjunction`) and `style` (`long`/`short`/`narrow`) behave exactly as the platform defines them. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-list.ts)
- `formatRelativeTime(value, locale, options)` computes a distance from `new Date()` and picks the largest non-zero unit in the order year, month, week, day, hour, minute, second, using fixed 30-day months and 365-day years, then formats through `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` with the sign of the difference. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-relative-time.ts)
- `formatTime(value, locale, options)` accepts either a `Date` or an `"H:m[:s]"` string, returns `null` when the value cannot be interpreted, formats through `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with `hour12` derived from `format: "12h" | "24h"`, and in 12h mode rewrites the `dayPeriod` part with `amLabel`/`pmLabel` when supplied. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-time.ts)
- `formatDate(date, format, locale, timeZone?)` implements a subset of the Unicode date field symbol table by iterating a fixed `FORMATS` list and replacing each token with `toLocaleString` output; tokens absent from that list are left in the output verbatim. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-date.ts)
- `isRTL(locale)` maximizes the locale with `Intl.Locale` and tests the resolved script against a 12-entry RTL script set, falling back to a 19-entry language-code set when `Intl.Locale` is unavailable; `getLocaleDir(locale)` returns `"rtl"` or `"ltr"`. Neither is covered by a test in this package. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/is-rtl.ts)

### RTL and i18n

- Given the list `["react", "svelte", "vue"]`, when `formatList` runs with `en-US` and no options, then the result is "react, svelte, and vue" with the Oxford comma, while `fr-FR` gives "react, svelte et vue" with no comma before the conjunction. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-list.test.ts: "conjunction / and")
- Given the same list and `style: "short"`, when `formatList` runs with `en-US`, then the conjunction becomes the ampersand "react, svelte, & vue", while `fr-FR` output is unchanged from its long form because French has no distinct short conjunction. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-list.test.ts: "conjunction / and + short")
- Given `style: "short"` and `type: "disjunction"`, when `formatList` runs with `en-US`, then the result is "react, svelte, or vue", so disjunction ignores the short style's ampersand substitution. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-list.test.ts: "disjunction / or")
- Given 1500 bytes, when `formatBytes` runs with `de-DE`, then the result is "1,5 kB" with a decimal comma; with `fr-FR` it is "1,5 ko" because French localises the byte unit to "octet"; with `ja-JP` and 1500000 it is "1.5 MB". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format with different locales")
- Given a 13:05 time and locale `ar-EG` in 12h mode, when `formatTime` runs, then the result is "١:٠٥ م" with Arabic-Indic digits and the Arabic PM marker, so the numbering system and day period both follow the locale. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats 12h times with locale day period in other locales")
- Given a 09:07:03 `Date` and locale `ar-EG` in 24h mode with seconds, when `formatTime` runs, then the result is "٠٩:٠٧:٠٣" in Arabic-Indic digits. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats 24h times with seconds in other locales")
- Given the string "9:7:3" and locale `fa-IR` in 24h mode with seconds, when `formatTime` runs, then the result is "۰۹:۰۷:۰۳" in extended Arabic-Indic (Persian) digits, so string parsing feeds the same locale-aware number formatting as `Date` input. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats string times in other locales")
- Given the format token pairs "EEEE, MMMM D, yyyy", when `formatDate` runs with `en-US` on 2022-01-01, then the result is "Saturday, January 1, 2022", so weekday and month names come from `toLocaleString` and follow the locale. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "should handle different locales")

### Notes and edge cases

- Given `NaN`, when `formatBytes` runs, then it returns the empty string rather than "NaN B". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should return empty string for NaN")
- Given 0, when `formatBytes` runs, then it returns the hardcoded literal "0 B", which is the only output that bypasses `Intl.NumberFormat` and therefore the only one that ignores locale and `unitDisplay`. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should return '0 B' for 0 bytes")
- Given a negative byte count, when `formatBytes` runs, then the unit is chosen from the absolute value and the sign is restored, giving "-1.5 kB" for -1500 and "-1 MB" for -1048576 in binary mode. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle negative values")
- Given 1, 0.5, or 100 bytes, when `formatBytes` runs with the default short unit display, then the results are "1 byte", "0.5 byte", and "100 byte", so the short display uses the singular "byte" for every count and never pluralises. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle very small values")
- Given `Infinity` or `-Infinity`, when `formatBytes` runs, then the division loop runs out of prefixes and the result is "∞ PB" or "-∞ PB" rather than an error. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle Infinity")
- Given 1500 with `unit: "byte"` and `unitDisplay: "short"`, when `formatBytes` runs in decimal mode, then the result is "1.5 kB" with a lowercase SI kilo prefix. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format bytes correctly")
- Given 1500 with `unit: "bit"`, when `formatBytes` runs in decimal mode, then the result is "1.5 kb" with a lowercase b, distinguishing bits from bytes only by unit case. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format bits correctly")
- Given 1500000000, when `formatBytes` runs in decimal mode, then the result is "1.5 GB". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle large byte values")
- Given 1e15, 1.5e15, and 2.5e15, when `formatBytes` runs in decimal mode, then the results are "1 PB", "1.5 PB", and "2.5 PB", confirming petabyte is the top byte prefix. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle very large values (petabyte)")
- Given the decimal boundary values 999, 1000, 999999, and 1000000, when `formatBytes` runs, then the results are "999 byte", "1 kB", "1,000 kB", and "1 MB"; 999999 rounds up to "1,000 kB" instead of promoting to "1 MB" because precision is applied after the unit is chosen. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle boundary values")
- Given binary-sized inputs formatted in decimal mode (1024, 1048576, 1073741824, 1099511627776 and each value one byte lower), when `formatBytes` runs, then the results are "1.02 kB", "1.05 MB", "1.07 GB", and "1.1 TB", with the off-by-one inputs producing identical strings because 3 significant digits hide the difference. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "sink")
- Given 1234567 and precision 1, 2, 3, or 5, when `formatBytes` runs, then the results are "1 MB", "1.2 MB", "1.23 MB", and "1.235 MB"; the comment notes `toPrecision(5)` yields 1.2346 but `Intl.NumberFormat` rounds it again to 1.235, so precision is not a faithful significant-digit count. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should respect different precision values")
- Given 1234567 and precision 4, when `formatBytes` runs, then the result is "1.235 MB" because `toPrecision` rounds up. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle precision with toPrecision rounding")
- Given `unitDisplay: "long"`, when `formatBytes` formats 1500 and 1500000, then the results are "1.5 kilobytes" and "1.5 megabytes", so the long display does pluralise where the short display does not. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format with long unit display")
- Given `unitDisplay: "short"`, when `formatBytes` formats 1500 and 1500000, then the results are "1.5 kB" and "1.5 MB" with a space before the unit. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format with short unit display")
- Given `unitDisplay: "narrow"`, when `formatBytes` formats 1500 and 1500000, then the results are "1.5kB" and "1.5MB" with no space at all. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format with narrow unit display")
- Given `unit: "bit"` and inputs 1500, 1500000, 1500000000, and 1500000000000, when `formatBytes` runs, then the results scale through "1.5 kb", "1.5 Mb", "1.5 Gb", and "1.5 Tb", terabit being the largest bit prefix available. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format bits with different scales")
- Given 1536 with `unitSystem: "binary"`, when `formatBytes` runs, then the result is "1.5 kB" for bytes and "1.5 kb" for bits, so binary mode reuses the decimal SI unit names rather than emitting KiB or Kib. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format bytes correctly"; zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should format bits correctly")
- Given 1610612736 with `unitSystem: "binary"`, when `formatBytes` runs, then the result is "1.5 GB". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle large byte values")
- Given `Math.pow(1024, 5)` and its 1.5x and 2x multiples with `unitSystem: "binary"`, when `formatBytes` runs, then the results are "1 PB", "1.5 PB", and "2 PB". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle very large binary values (petabyte)")
- Given binary boundary values 1023, 1024, and 1025, when `formatBytes` runs in binary mode, then the results are "1,020 byte", "1 kB", and "1 kB"; 1023 stays in bytes but is rounded to 1020 by the 3-digit precision, producing a grouped-thousands byte count. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "should handle boundary values")
- Given a spread of binary inputs including 1075200, 1148903751, 1209462790553, 1022, 1018 at precision 2, and the values one below each power of 1024, when `formatBytes` runs in binary mode, then the outputs are "1.03 MB", "1.07 GB", "1.1 TB", "1,020 byte", "1,000 byte", and the sub-boundary values collapse to "1,020 kB", "1,020 MB", and "1,020 GB", so a value one byte short of the next unit reads as a four-digit count of the smaller unit. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts: "sink")
- Given `MockDate` pinning now to 2024-01-01 and a date two months earlier, when `formatRelativeTime` runs with `en-US`, then the result is "2 months ago", and with `style: "narrow"` it is "2mo ago". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-relative-time.test.ts: "months")
- Given now pinned to 2024-01-01 and a date two days later, when `formatRelativeTime` runs, then the result is the future-tense "in 2 days", and with narrow style "in 2d", so the sign of the difference selects tense. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-relative-time.test.ts: "days")
- Given now pinned to 2024-01-01 and a date two seconds earlier, when `formatRelativeTime` runs, then the result is "2 seconds ago", and with narrow style "2s ago". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-relative-time.test.ts: "secs")
- No test covers the singular plural forms ("1 day ago", "in 1 month"), the zero case, the week branch, or the hour and minute branches of `formatRelativeTime`, so those units and the English plural rules are unverified. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-relative-time.ts)
- Given a `Date` at 04:05:06 and `format: "24h"`, when `formatTime` runs with `en-US`, then the result is "04:05" with a zero-padded hour and no seconds. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats 24h time from date")
- Given the unpadded string "4:5:6" with `withSeconds: true`, when `formatTime` runs in 24h mode, then the result is "04:05:06", so all three segments are zero-padded on output. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats 24h time with seconds from string")
- Given a 13:05 `Date` and `format: "12h"`, when `formatTime` runs with `en-US`, then the result is "1:05 PM" with an unpadded hour and the locale day period. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "formats 12h time with locale day period")
- Given a 13:05 `Date` with `amLabel: "morning"` and `pmLabel: "evening"`, when `formatTime` runs in 12h mode, then only the `dayPeriod` token is substituted and the result is "1:05 evening". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "uses custom AM/PM labels when provided")
- Given the unparsable "invalid", the out-of-range hour "25:00", or the out-of-range minute "12:70", when `formatTime` runs, then it returns `null` for each rather than throwing or clamping. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "returns null for invalid time strings")
- Given the string "04:05:06" with `withSeconds` left at its default false, when `formatTime` runs in 24h mode, then the seconds are dropped and the result is "04:05". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "omits seconds when withSeconds is false")
- Given the string "4:5" with no seconds segment and `withSeconds: true`, when `formatTime` runs, then the missing seconds default to zero and the result is "04:05:00". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts: "pads seconds when missing and withSeconds is true")
- Every `formatTime` assertion routes the output through a `normalize` helper that replaces U+00A0 and U+202F with a plain space, because modern ICU emits a narrow no-break space before the day period; without that step the same expectations fail across Node and browser Intl versions. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-time.test.ts)
- Given the format string "yyyy-MM-DD" on 2022-01-01, when `formatDate` runs with `en-US`, then the result is "2022-01-01". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "should format date correctly")
- Given the format string "yyyy-MM-DD HH:mm:ss" on a 13:15:30 date, when `formatDate` runs, then every token is replaced in one pass and the result is "2022-01-01 13:15:30". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "should replace all format keys in the format string")
- Given the day tokens on January 1, when `formatDate` runs, then "d" gives "1", "do" gives "1st", "dd" gives "01", "D" gives "1", "Do" gives "1st", "DD" gives "01", and "DDD" gives "001" (day of month padded to three, not day of year). (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format day")
- Given the unsupported tokens "ddd", "dddd", and "DDDD", when `formatDate` runs, then they are echoed back literally as "ddd", "dddd", and "DDDD" because they are absent from the `FORMATS` table, so a typo in a format string silently ends up in the output. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format day")
- Given the month tokens on January, when `formatDate` runs, then "M" gives "1", "Mo" gives "1st", "MM" gives "01", "MMM" gives "Jan", "MMMM" gives "January", and "MMMMM" gives the narrow "J". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format month")
- Given the year tokens on 2022, when `formatDate` runs, then "y"/"Y"/"yyyy"/"YYY"/"YYYY" all give "2022", "yy"/"YY" give "22", and "yo"/"Yo" give the nonsensical ordinal "2022nd" because the ordinal helper is applied to the full year. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format year")
- Given a 04:15 time, when `formatDate` runs the hour tokens, then "h" gives "4 AM" and "hh" gives "04 AM" because the 12-hour `toLocaleString` call carries the day period along with the hour, while "H" and "HH" give "04" and "ho"/"Ho" give "4th". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format hour")
- Given a minute value of 15, when `formatDate` runs, then "m" gives "15", "mo" gives "15th", and "mm" gives "15", so the 2-digit minute token does not actually pad a two-digit value differently from the numeric one. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format minute")
- Given January (Q1), when `formatDate` runs the quarter tokens, then "Q" gives "1", "Qo" gives "1st", "QQ" gives "01", "QQQQ" gives "1st quarter" (hardcoded English, not localised), and "QQQQQ" gives "1". (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format quarter")
- Given day 1 of the month, when `formatDate` runs the week tokens, then "w" gives "1", "wo" gives "1st", and "ww" gives "01"; the implementation computes `ceil(dayOfMonth / 7)`, so this is a week-of-month approximation and not the ISO week of year. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format week"; zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-date.ts)
- Given a Saturday, when `formatDate` runs the weekday tokens, then "E"/"EE"/"EEE" all give "Sat", "EEEE" gives "Saturday", "EEEEE" gives the narrow "S", and "EEEEEE" gives "Sa" produced by slicing the short form to two characters rather than by an Intl width. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format weekday")
- The timezone token test is `test.skip`, so "z", "zz", "zzz", and "zzzz" are not actually verified; the source marks the zone branch with a "TODO: Revise this" and extracts the zone by splitting the formatted string on AM/PM, which throws for 24-hour locales. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts: "format timezone"; zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/src/format-date.ts)
- The `formatDate` fixture is built with the local-time `Date` constructor and the era, day period ("a" family), and "T" timestamp tokens are never asserted, so era handling and the timestamp path are unverified and the hour assertions depend on the runner's time zone. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-date.test.ts)
- Every `formatBytes` and `formatList` expectation is an inline snapshot of host ICU output, so unit names, grouping separators, and the French "ko" abbreviation can shift with the Node or browser Intl version; the byte test file even disables the `no-irregular-whitespace` lint rule because the snapshots contain non-ASCII spaces. (zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-byte.test.ts; zag: packages/utilities/i18n-utils/tests/format-list.test.ts)

## color-utils

### Roles and attributes

- The package exports no DOM parts. Its public surface is `parseColor(value)`, `normalizeColor(value)` (a pass-through for an existing `ColorType`), the abstract `Color` base class, and `getColorAreaGradient`. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/index.ts)
- `parseColor(value)` first looks the string up in the CSS named-colour map, then tries `RGBColor.parse`, then `HSBColor.parse`, then `HSLColor.parse`, and throws `Invalid color value: <value>` (with `Error.captureStackTrace` trimming its own frame) when all three fail. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/parse-color.ts)
- The named-colour table holds 140-odd CSS colour keywords as hex strings and additionally registers a `grey` spelling for every `gray` key (so `darkgrey`, `dimgrey`, `slategrey` all resolve), then recurses through `parseColor` on the hex value. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/native-color.ts)
- `RGBColor.parse` accepts `#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`, and `#rrggbbaa` (gating on lengths 4, 5, 7, and 9 and doubling each nibble for the short forms, with the fourth byte divided by 255 to become alpha), plus `rgb(r, g, b)` and `rgba(r, g, b, a)` with the first three components clamped to 0-255 and alpha clamped to 0-1; alpha defaults to 1 when absent. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts)
- `HSLColor.parse` and `HSBColor.parse` match `hsl(...)`/`hsla(...)` and `hsb(...)`/`hsba(...)` with signed decimal hue and percent saturation and lightness or brightness; hue is wrapped with `mod(h, 360)` rather than clamped, saturation and lightness or brightness are clamped to 0-100, and alpha is clamped to 0-1 defaulting to 1. Neither regex accepts the modern space-separated or `deg`-suffixed CSS syntax. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsl-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsb-color.ts)
- `toFormat(format)` converts between `"rgba"`, `"hsla"`, and `"hsba"`, returning `this` for a no-op conversion and throwing `Unsupported color conversion: <from> -> <to>` for anything else, so every colour object can reach every other model in one hop. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsl-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsb-color.ts)
- `toString(format)` supports `"css"`, `"hex"`, `"hexa"`, `"rgb"`, `"rgba"`, `"hsl"`, `"hsla"`, `"hsb"`, and `"hsba"`; `"css"` resolves to `rgba(...)` from an RGB colour, to `hsla(...)` from an HSL colour, and to the HSL `css` form from an HSB colour, so HSB never round-trips to a `hsb()` string through `"css"`. Hex output is uppercased and zero-padded per byte. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsl-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsb-color.ts)
- Channel ranges drive keyboard stepping: red, green, and blue are 0-255 with step 1 and pageSize 17 (`0x11`), hue is 0-360 with step 1 and pageSize 15, saturation and lightness or brightness are 0-100 with step 1 and pageSize 10, and alpha is 0-1 with step 0.01 and pageSize 0.1. An unknown channel name throws `Unknown color channel: <name>`. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsl-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/hsb-color.ts)
- `Color` supplies the shared behaviour: `getChannelValue` throws `Unsupported color channel` for a channel the subclass lacks, `withChannelValue` clones and clamps, `getChannelValuePercent`/`getChannelPercentValue` map between raw values and 0-1 fractions with step snapping, `incrementChannel(channel, stepSize)` clamps then snaps to the channel step, `decrementChannel` delegates to `incrementChannel` with a negated step, `getColorAxes` fills in the missing x, y, and z channels for a 2D area, `toHexInt` routes through the RGB model, and `isEqual` compares `toJSON()` key-by-key plus the alpha channel. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/color.ts)
- RGB to HSB and RGB to HSL use the Wikipedia conversion formulas and round every output channel with `toFixedNumber(..., 2)`, so a conversion is lossy at the second decimal place and repeated round-trips accumulate that rounding. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts)
- `formatChannelValue(channel, locale)` formats red, green, and blue as `style: "decimal"` and alpha as `style: "percent"` through `Intl.NumberFormat`, so channel readouts are locale-aware. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/rgb-color.ts)

### Notes and edge cases

- Given the hex string "#361717", when it is parsed and converted with `toFormat("hsla")`, then the result is the HSL object `{ h: 0, s: 40.26, l: 15.1, a: 1 }`, pinning the hex-to-RGB-to-HSL chain and its two-decimal rounding. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "decrement")
- Given that HSL colour, when `decrementChannel("saturation", 1)` runs, then saturation goes from 40.26 to 39 rather than 39.26, because the result is snapped to the channel's step of 1 after clamping; hue, lightness, and alpha are untouched. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "decrement")
- Given that same HSL colour, when `decrementChannel("lightness", 1)` runs, then lightness goes from 15.1 to 14 (again snapped to the step grid) and saturation stays at its fractional 40.26, confirming each call operates on the original colour rather than a mutated one. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "decrement")
- Given the CSS strings "hsl(0, 92%, 13%)" and "hsl(0, 76%, 31%)", when `parseColor` runs, then each yields an HSL colour with the percent signs stripped and alpha defaulted to 1, giving `{ h: 0, s: 92, l: 13, a: 1 }` and `{ h: 0, s: 76, l: 31, a: 1 }`; the test is named "hexint" but never calls `toHexInt`. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "hexint")
- Both tests assert with `toMatchInlineSnapshot` against the short-key JSON shape (`h`, `s`, `l`, `a`), so the snapshots pin the serialised representation rather than the public getters and break if the JSON key names change. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "decrement"; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts: "hexint")
- The suite covers only two cases in total, so none of the following are verified anywhere in this package: hex parsing of the 3-digit and 8-digit short forms, alpha extraction from `#rrggbbaa`, `rgb()`/`rgba()` parsing and its 0-255 clamping, `hsb()`/`hsba()` parsing, hue wrap-around via `mod`, named-colour lookup and the gray/grey aliasing, the `Invalid color value` throw path, round-trips in either direction between hex, rgb, hsl, and hsb, every `toString` format including `"hex"`, `"hexa"`, and `"css"`, `toHexInt`, `isEqual`, `incrementChannel`, `withChannelValue`, `getColorAxes`, `formatChannelValue`, the `Unknown color channel` and `Unsupported color conversion` throws, `normalizeColor`, `getColorAreaGradient`, and the format-gradient helpers. (zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/tests/color.test.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/parse-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/native-color.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/area-gradient.ts; zag: packages/utilities/color-utils/src/color-format-gradient.ts)

## rect-utils

### Notes and edge cases

- The package exposes `createRect`, `getRectFromPoints`, `getRectCorners`, `containsPoint`, `intersection`, `intersects`, `collisions`, `inset` and `union`. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/src)
- Given `{ x: 0, y: 0, width: 100, height: 100 }`, then `createRect` returns a rect carrying those four values. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "should create rect")
- Given five points describing a 10 by 50 box, then `getRectFromPoints` derives width 10, height 50, `minX`/`minY` 0, `maxX` 10, `maxY` 50, `midX`/`midY` 5 and 25, and a `center` of (5, 25); `getRectCorners` on that rect returns top (0,0), right (10,0), bottom (10,50) and left (0,50); and `containsPoint` is true for a point on the right edge at (10, 25). (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "should create rect from point")
- Given an 80 by 100 rect at the origin and a 50 by 45 rect at (60, 20), then `intersection` returns the 20 by 45 overlap at (60, 20) and `intersects` is true. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "should get the intersection of two rects")
- Given a 20 by 20 rect at (20, 10) inside a 40 by 30 boundary, then `collisions` reports `right` and `bottom` as the colliding edges. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "should get the collision edges between rects")
- Given a 40 by 30 rect, then `inset` with a negative dx grows it symmetrically on the x axis to width 60 at x -10, and a positive dx shrinks it to width 30 at x 5, leaving y and height untouched. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "grow rect"; zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "shrink rect")
- Given two rects that touch at y 30, then `union` returns the 40 by 50 bounding box at the origin. (zag: packages/utilities/rect/tests/rect.test.ts: "merges rects")

## number-utils

### Notes and edge cases

- Given floating-point steps, then `incrementValue` avoids binary drift: 1.123 plus 0.004 is exactly 1.127, 12.01 plus 0.04 is 12.05, and 12.05 plus 0.05 is 12.1. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/number.test.ts: "increment")
- Given 12.015 minus 0.004, then `decrementValue` returns exactly 12.011 rather than a drifting float. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/number.test.ts: "decrement")
- Given a value above the max with a step larger than the whole range, then `snapValueToStep` clamps to the max (240 in 0-100 with step 200 gives 100), and a value below the min clamps to the min (-50 gives 0). (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/number.test.ts: "snapValueToStep")
- Given values inside the range, then `snapValueToStep` rounds to the nearest step (23 gives 20, 27 gives 30), leaves an exact step boundary alone (50 gives 50), and clamps 150 to the max 100 when the step divides the range evenly. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/number.test.ts: "snapValueToStep")
- Given primitives, then `isEqual` is true for identical numbers, strings and booleans and false for differing ones. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should return true for equal primitive values"; zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should return false for unequal primitive values")
- Given two structurally identical objects, then `isEqual` is true, and false when any value differs. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should return true for equal object values"; zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should return false for unequal object values")
- Given nested objects such as `{ positioning: { placement: "start" } }`, then `isEqual` compares deeply. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should check deep object values")
- Given a plain object and a Proxy wrapping an identical object, then `isEqual` is true, which matters because Zag's store hands out proxies. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should compare with proxy")
- Given two arrays holding the same objects in a different order, then `isEqual` is false, so array equality is positional. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/equal.test.ts: "should respect positional equality")
- Given an object with `undefined` values at any depth, then `compact` removes those keys while keeping the rest, including nested objects. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/object.test.ts: "should compact object")
- Given `null` values, then `compact` preserves them, so null is a meaningful value and only undefined is dropped. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/object.test.ts: "should preserve null")
- Given `splitProps(props, ["a", "c"])`, then it returns the picked object and the remainder as a pair. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/object.test.ts: "should split props")
- Given a key that does not exist on the props, then `splitProps` returns an empty picked object and the untouched rest rather than an object with undefined keys. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/object.test.ts: "should handle missing keys gracefully")
- Given symbol keys among the props, then `splitProps` keeps them in the correct half, which is what makes Svelte attachments survive prop splitting. (zag: packages/utilities/core/tests/object.test.ts: "should perserve symbol keys")

## file-utils

### Notes and edge cases

- The package exposes `isValidFileType(file, accept)` returning a `[valid, error]` pair and `createFileTypeValidator(accept)` returning a reusable predicate. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/src/is-valid-file-type.ts)
- Given `accept` is undefined, an empty string or an empty array, then every file is accepted. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "accepts everything when accept is empty")
- Given an exact mime type, then only a file with that type matches. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "matches an exact mime type")
- Given a wildcard mime type such as `image/*`, then any file in that family matches and others do not. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "matches a wildcard mime type")
- Given an extension such as `.png` or `.gz`, then matching is done on the file name, so `archive.tar.gz` matches `.gz`. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "matches an extension")
- Given differing case on either side (`IMAGE/*`, `a.PNG`, `.PNG`), then matching is case insensitive. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "is case insensitive on both sides")
- Given a comma separated accept string with surrounding whitespace, then each entry is trimmed before matching. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "handles a comma separated list with surrounding whitespace")
- Given a file with an empty `type`, then the extension is used instead, and a file with neither a type nor an extension fails a mime-only accept list. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "falls back to the extension when the file has no type")
- Given a file whose type is `application/x-moz-file`, then it is always accepted, because that is Firefox's directory placeholder and rejecting it would break directory uploads. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "always accepts the firefox directory placeholder")
- Given an array of accept entries mixing mime types and extensions (including padded ones), then any entry may match. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "accepts an array of types")
- Given a validation result, then it is the pair `[true, null]` on success and `[false, "FILE_INVALID_TYPE"]` on failure, which is the error code the file-upload machine surfaces. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "reports the error alongside the result")
- Given two validators created from different accept strings, then they do not share state and repeated calls stay stable. (zag: packages/utilities/file-utils/tests/is-valid-file-type.test.ts: "validators are independent")

## highlight-word

### Notes and edge cases

- The package exposes `highlightWord({ text, query, matchAll, ignoreCase, exactMatch })` returning an array of `{ text, match }` chunks, built on `highlightFirst`, `highlightMultiple`, `normalizeSpan` and `escapeRegex`. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/src/highlight.ts; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/src/escape-regex.ts)
- Given "Hello world" and the query "world", then the result is two chunks, the non-matching "Hello " and the matching "world". (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "works")
- Given `ignoreCase: false` and a query whose case differs from the text, then nothing matches and the whole text is one non-matching chunk; with `ignoreCase: true` the original casing of the matched text is preserved in the chunk. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "case sensitivity"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "ignoring case")
- Given a query that does not occur, or an empty query, then the whole text is returned as a single non-matching chunk. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "query is not found"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "empty query")
- Given a match at the very start or the very end of the text, then no empty leading or trailing chunk is emitted. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "query at the beginning"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "query at the end")
- Given an array query while `matchAll` is false, then it throws, so multi-term queries require the match-all mode. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "throw when query is array and matchAll is false")
- Given `exactMatch: true`, then a query that only appears as a prefix of a longer word does not match ("quick" against "quickly"), while a standalone word does, splitting the text into three chunks. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "not exact match partial words"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match complete words")
- Given `exactMatch` combined with case options, then a case mismatch yields no match with `ignoreCase: false` and matches while preserving the text's casing with `ignoreCase: true`. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match without ignore case"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match with ignore case")
- Given `matchAll: true` and a single query, then every occurrence becomes its own matching chunk. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "works"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "applies to all matches")
- Given `matchAll: true` and an array query, then each term is highlighted wherever it occurs. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "array query")
- Given `matchAll: true` with a case-differing query, then the case rules match the single-occurrence behavior. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "case sensitivity")
- Given a query containing regex-significant characters such as "(quick)", then it is escaped and matched literally. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "special characters in query")
- Given a query that is itself a regex such as "(.)+", then it is not interpreted as a pattern and matches nothing. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "does not parse regex characters")
- Given `matchAll: true` with an empty query, or a query longer than the text, then the text is returned unmatched. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "empty query"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "query longer than text")
- Given an array query containing empty strings, then the empty entries are filtered out and only the real terms are highlighted. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "filter empty items in query")
- Given `exactMatch` with `matchAll`, then partial-word occurrences are skipped while the standalone occurrence is highlighted, including across an array query with and without ignoreCase. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "not exact match partial words"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match without ignore case"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match with ignore case"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match with array query"; zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match with array query and ignore case")
- Given punctuation next to a word, then exact matching treats punctuation as a word boundary, so "world" matches in both "Hello, world!" and "The world is nice." (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts: "exact match with punctuation boundaries")
- Every case asserts with `toMatchInlineSnapshot` over the chunk array, so the chunk shape (`text` plus boolean `match`) and the exact segmentation are both pinned. (zag: packages/utilities/highlight-word/tests/highlight-word.test.ts)

## scroll-snap

### Notes and edge cases

- The package exposes `getSnapPositions(parent, subtree?)`, `getScrollSnapPositions(element)`, `findSnapPoint(parent, axis, predicate)` and `getSnapPointTarget(parent, snapPoint)`; the carousel machine is built on these. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/src/index.ts)
- Given three 100px items aligned start, center and end, then `getSnapPositions` reports the raw measurement points 0, 150 and 300 in their respective alignment buckets. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "collects positions per alignment")
- Given an item with `scroll-snap-align: none`, then it contributes no snap position in any bucket. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "skips items with align none")
- Given `direction: rtl`, then offsets are measured from the right edge, so four start-aligned items report 0, 100, 200, 300 counting leftward. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "measures from the right edge in RTL")
- Given four 100px items in a 200px viewport, then `getScrollSnapPositions` converts start alignment into scroll offsets clamped to the 200px max scroll, giving 0, 100, 200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "returns start positions clamped to max scroll")
- Given center alignment, then each position is the item center minus half the viewport, clamped into range, giving 0, 50, 150, 200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "offsets center positions by half the container size")
- Given end alignment, then each position is the item end minus the viewport, clamped and deduped, giving 0, 100, 200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "offsets end positions by the container size")
- Given `scroll-padding-left: 10px`, then each snap offset is inset by 10, giving 0, 90, 190, 200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "applies scroll padding")
- Given a percentage scroll padding, then it resolves against the container size, so 10 percent of a 200px viewport insets by 20. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "resolves percentage scroll padding against the container size")
- Given RTL with the negative `scrollLeft` convention used by Chrome and Safari, then positions are negated, giving -0, -100, -200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "negates positions in RTL with negative scrollLeft behavior")
- Given a vertically scrolling container, then the same math is applied on the y axis. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "supports the vertical axis")
- Given a predicate selecting one child, then `findSnapPoint` returns that child's scroll position for its alignment: 200 for start, 150 for center (raw 250 minus half the viewport) and 100 for end (raw 300 minus the viewport). (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "returns the start-aligned position of the matching item"; zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "offsets center-aligned items by half the container size"; zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "offsets end-aligned items by the container size")
- Given scroll padding, then `findSnapPoint` applies it per alignment: a start-aligned item with 10px left padding resolves to 90 and an end-aligned item with 10px right padding to 110. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "applies scroll padding per alignment")
- Given the first or last item under center alignment, then the result is clamped to 0 and to the max scroll of 200. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "clamps to the scrollable range")
- Given RTL, then `findSnapPoint` returns -100 under the negative `scrollLeft` convention and +100 when the container reports the positive convention, detected from the initial scroll offset; this is a genuine cross-browser difference. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "negates positions in RTL with negative scrollLeft behavior"; zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "returns positive positions in RTL with positive scrollLeft behavior")
- Given the vertical axis, then `findSnapPoint` behaves the same on y. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "supports the vertical axis")
- Given a predicate that matches nothing, then `findSnapPoint` returns undefined. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "returns undefined when no item matches")
- Given each of the three alignments, then every value `findSnapPoint` returns is also present in `getScrollSnapPositions`, so the two APIs cannot disagree. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "agrees with getScrollSnapPositions for %s alignment")
- Given a snap point, then `getSnapPointTarget` returns the child whose snap position matches it, and falls back to the first child when nothing matches. (zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "returns the child whose snap position matches the snap point"; zag: packages/utilities/scroll-snap/tests/scroll-snap.test.ts: "falls back to the first child when nothing matches")

## auto-resize

### Notes and edge cases

- `autoresizeTextarea(el)` patches the textarea so height tracks content and returns a cleanup function; the tests pair it with a `trackValue` helper that models a framework's value tracker. (zag: packages/utilities/auto-resize/src)
- Given the utility is attached, when the textarea's `value` property is written programmatically, then no synthetic `input` event is dispatched, so a controlled component cannot be tricked into an update loop. (zag: packages/utilities/auto-resize/tests/autoresize-textarea.test.ts: "programmatic value writes do not dispatch input events")
- Given the utility is attached, when `value` is written programmatically, then the framework value tracker still sees the new value, which is what keeps React-style change detection honest. (zag: packages/utilities/auto-resize/tests/autoresize-textarea.test.ts: "programmatic value writes keep the framework value tracker in sync")
- Given a controlled textarea that rejects digits and resets its value, when a digit is typed, then onChange fires exactly once with the rejected value and the element ends up empty, so a rejecting controlled component does not produce a second spurious change. (zag: packages/utilities/auto-resize/tests/autoresize-textarea.test.ts: "controlled textarea that rejects input fires onChange once per keystroke")
- Given a controlled textarea cleared programmatically after a keystroke, when the same character is typed again, then onChange fires a second time with that character, so clearing does not leave stale tracker state that swallows the next identical input. (zag: packages/utilities/auto-resize/tests/autoresize-textarea.test.ts: "clearing a controlled textarea programmatically keeps change detection working")

## hotkeys

### Keyboard

- Given the hotkey string "mod++" parsed for the mac platform, when parseHotkey runs, then mod resolves to Meta (meta true, ctrl false), keys is ["+"], and codes is ["Equal"] because "+" sits on the same physical key as "=". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse mod++ correctly on mac")
- Given the hotkey string "mod++" parsed for the windows platform, when parseHotkey runs, then mod resolves to Control (ctrl true, meta false), keys is ["+"] and codes is ["Equal"]. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse mod++ correctly on windows")
- Given the hotkey string "Control++" on windows, when parseHotkey runs, then the trailing empty segment from the consecutive "+" characters is treated as the start of the key, so ctrl is true and the key is the literal "+" rather than an empty key. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse Control++ correctly")
- Given the hotkey string "+" alone, when parseHotkey runs, then no modifier flags are set, keys is ["+"] and codes is ["Equal"]. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse simple + key")
- Given the hotkey string "mod+S" on mac, when parseHotkey runs, then meta is true, keys is ["S"] and codes is ["KeyS"]. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse mod+S correctly")
- Given a hotkey string that is a single bare modifier name ("shift", "ctrl", "alt", "meta"), when parseHotkey runs, then keys is empty and only the matching modifier flag is set, so a lone modifier is never mistaken for an action key. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should parse a lone modifier as a modifier, not a key")
- Given the bare modifier "Shift" written with a capital, when parseHotkey runs, then it is still recognized as the Shift modifier, so lone modifier names are case insensitive. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should be case insensitive for lone modifiers")
- Given the bare alias "mod", when parseHotkey runs for mac then meta is set, and when it runs for windows then ctrl is set, so the platform alias resolves even with no action key. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should resolve a lone mod per platform")
- Given a single non-modifier character such as "k", when parseHotkey runs, then it is treated as the key (normalized to "K") and no modifier flag is set. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should still treat non-modifier single keys as keys")
- Given two hotkey strings that mean the same chord written differently ("mod+k" against "Meta+K" on mac, "mod+k" against "Control+K" on windows, "ctrl+shift+k" against "Shift+Control+K"), when normalizeHotkey runs on each, then both produce the identical canonical string. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should produce the same string for equivalent hotkeys")
- Given the hotkey "shift+ctrl+alt+meta+k" in arbitrary modifier order, when normalizeHotkey runs, then the output is exactly "Control+Alt+Shift+Meta+K", fixing the canonical modifier order as Control, Alt, Shift, Meta followed by the keys. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should order modifiers canonically"; zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/src/parser.ts)
- Given sequence strings "g > h" and "G>H", when normalizeHotkey runs, then both produce "G > H", so surrounding whitespace around the ">" separator is normalized to a single space on each side. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should normalize sequences")
- Given the bare modifier "shift", when normalizeHotkey runs, then the output is "Shift" with no trailing separator or key. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should normalize a bare modifier")
- Given the pairs ("mod+k","Meta+K"), ("ctrl+shift+k","Shift+Control+K") and ("g > h","G>H"), when normalizeHotkey equality is compared against isHotkeyEqual for each pair, then the two agree, so the canonical string is a valid identity key for a registered hotkey. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should agree with isHotkeyEqual")
- Given hotkeys that differ in the action key ("mod+k" against "mod+j") or in the modifier ("ctrl+k" against "meta+k" on mac), when normalizeHotkey runs, then the canonical strings differ. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/parser.test.ts: "should distinguish different hotkeys")
- Given a lowercase single letter, when normalizeKey runs, then it is uppercased ("a" to "A", "z" to "Z", "m" to "M"). (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should uppercase lowercase letters")
- Given an already uppercase single letter, when normalizeKey runs, then it is returned unchanged. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should preserve uppercase letters")
- Given the empty string, a digit "1", or the symbol "!", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned unchanged, so digits are not uppercased and symbols are preserved. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should handle single letter edge cases")
- Given "backspace", "Backspace" or "BACKSPACE", when normalizeKey runs, then all three produce "Backspace", so alias lookup is case insensitive. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize backspace variants")
- Given "tab" or "Tab", when normalizeKey runs, then both produce "Tab". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize tab")
- Given "clear" or "Clear", when normalizeKey runs, then both produce "Clear". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize clear")
- Given "enter", "return", "Enter" or "Return", when normalizeKey runs, then all four produce "Enter", so "return" is an accepted alias for Enter. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize enter/return")
- Given "esc", "escape", "Esc" or "Escape", when normalizeKey runs, then all four produce "Escape". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize escape variants")
- Given "space", "spacebar", "Space" or "Spacebar", when normalizeKey runs, then all four produce the single space character " ", matching what browsers report as KeyboardEvent.key for the space bar. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize space variants")
- Given the arrow aliases "up"/"arrowup"/"Up"/"ArrowUp", "down"/"arrowdown"/"Down", "left"/"arrowleft"/"Left" and "right"/"arrowright"/"Right", when normalizeKey runs, then each group collapses to "ArrowUp", "ArrowDown", "ArrowLeft" and "ArrowRight". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize arrow keys")
- Given the aliases "pageup"/"pgup"/"PageUp", "pagedown"/"pgdn"/"PageDown", "home"/"Home" and "end"/"End", when normalizeKey runs, then each group collapses to "PageUp", "PageDown", "Home" and "End". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize page navigation keys")
- Given the aliases "del"/"delete"/"Del"/"Delete" and "ins"/"insert"/"Ins"/"Insert", when normalizeKey runs, then each group collapses to "Delete" and "Insert". (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize delete/insert keys")
- Given function key spellings f1 through f19 in either case, when normalizeKey runs, then the result is the uppercase form (F1, F10, F19), so function keys F1-F19 are recognized. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should normalize function keys F1-F19")
- Given "f20", "F20" or "f25", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned byte for byte unchanged (lowercase stays lowercase), so the normalization range deliberately stops at F19. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should not normalize F20 or higher")
- Given the malformed function-key spellings "f", "f0" and "fa", when normalizeKey runs, then "f" is uppercased to "F" by the single-letter rule while "f0" and "fa" are returned unchanged. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should not normalize invalid function key formats")
- Given already canonical keys "ArrowUp", "Backspace", "Enter" and " ", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned unchanged, so normalization is idempotent. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should preserve already normalized keys")
- Given the symbols "+", "-", "=", "@" and "#", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned unchanged. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should preserve special characters")
- Given the digit strings "1", "0" and the multi-digit "123", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned unchanged. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should preserve numbers")
- Given mixed-case multi-character words "SomeKey" and "camelCase", when normalizeKey runs, then the original casing is preserved because the browser is assumed to already report a correct key value. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should preserve mixed case words")
- Given the empty string, "a1" or "key.with.dots", when normalizeKey runs, then each is returned unchanged. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/normalize.test.ts: "should handle edge cases")
- Given the parsed hotkey "/" and a US-layout event with key "/" and code "Slash", when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches / on US keyboard")
- Given the parsed hotkey "Control+/" and a US event with key "/", code "Slash" and ctrlKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches Ctrl+/ on US keyboard")
- Given the parsed hotkey "mod+/" on mac and an event with key "/", code "Slash" and metaKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches because mod resolved to Meta. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches Mod+/ on Mac")
- Given the parsed hotkey "/" with no modifiers and an event with key "/" plus ctrlKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it does not match, because Ctrl is always treated as an intentional modifier even for symbol keys. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "does not match / when Ctrl is pressed (no Ctrl in hotkey)")
- Given the parsed hotkey "Control+S" and an event with the lowercase key "s", code "KeyS" and ctrlKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches because the event key is normalized to uppercase before comparison. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches letter keys with strict modifier check")
- Given the parsed hotkey "Control+S" and an event with ctrlKey and shiftKey both true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it does not match, so an unlisted extra Shift breaks a letter chord. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "does not match letter key when extra shift is pressed")
- Given the parsed hotkey "A" with no modifiers and an event with key "a" and shiftKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then it does not match, so letters require an exact modifier match. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "letter keys require exact modifier match")
- Given the parsed hotkey "Q" (code "KeyQ") and an AZERTY event where the physical KeyQ produces key "a", when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches through the physical code, so letter bindings are layout independent. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "letter key matches via physical code on different layout")
- Given the parsed hotkey "Enter" and an event with key "Enter" and code "Enter", when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches on every layout. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "Enter matches regardless of layout")
- Given the parsed hotkey "1" and an event with key "1" and code "Digit1", when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "digit keys match strictly")
- Given the parsed hotkey "1" and an event where Shift turned Digit1 into "!", when matchesHotkey runs, then it does not match, because digits take the strict non-symbol path and the extra Shift is disqualifying. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "digit key does not match when shift is extra")
- Given the parsed hotkeys "Control+/", "mod+/" (mac) and "Alt+/" and an event for "/" with no modifier held, when matchesHotkey runs, then none match, so a declared Ctrl, Meta or Alt on a symbol hotkey is still required. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "Ctrl+/ requires Ctrl to be pressed"; zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "Meta+/ requires Meta to be pressed"; zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "Alt+/ requires Alt to be pressed"; zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "Alt+/ does not match when Alt is not pressed")
- Given each of the symbol hotkeys ".", ",", ";", "'", "=" and "\\" and a US event carrying the matching key and code (Period, Comma, Semicolon, Quote, Equal, Backslash), when matchesHotkey runs, then each matches; this is a six-case table over the common punctuation keys. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches \".\" on US layout")
- Given each of those same six symbol hotkeys and an event carrying the right key but an unrelated code plus shiftKey true, when matchesHotkey runs, then each still matches, so a symbol hotkey matches on the produced character regardless of which physical key produced it and regardless of an extra Shift. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches \".\" when produced with Shift on international layout")
- Given the parsed hotkey "space" and an event with key " " and code "Space", when matchesHotkey runs, then it matches on any layout. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "matches space on any layout")
- Given the ASCII characters "a", "Z" and "7", when isSymbolKey runs, then all return false, so letters and digits take the strict matching path. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "treats ASCII letters and digits as non-symbols")
- Given the non-ASCII characters "ğ", "İ", "ы", "日" and "٣", when isSymbolKey runs, then all return false, so any single Unicode letter or number is matched strictly like ASCII rather than through the lenient symbol path. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "treats Unicode letters and numbers as non-symbols")
- Given the single characters "/", "@", " " and "€", when isSymbolKey runs, then all return true, so the space bar is classified as a symbol for matching purposes. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "treats single punctuation / symbols as symbols")
- Given the multi-character key names "Enter", "F1" and "ArrowUp", when isSymbolKey runs, then all return false because any key of length other than 1 is a named key. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/matching.test.ts: "treats named keys (length !== 1) as non-symbols")
- Given a store on document with one of the standard chords registered, when the main key is dispatched with the corresponding modifier flags set on the event, then the action fires exactly once; the table covers Control with C, X, V, Z, A, S, B, I, U, F, H, T, W, G, P and backtick, Control+Shift with Z, S, P, N and F, Alt+ArrowUp, Alt+ArrowDown and Shift+Enter (26 cases). (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "copy: Control+C")
- Given a store on document, when a modifier chord is triggered, then only the main key's event modifier flags matter and no separate keydown for the modifier key itself is needed, because the store matches on event.ctrlKey/shiftKey/altKey/metaKey rather than on tracked modifier keydowns. - Given a store on document with a single-key hotkey registered, when that key is dispatched, then the action fires once; the table covers "/", "?" (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "slash-search: /")
- Given a store on document with a function-key hotkey registered, when the key is dispatched (with a preceding modifier keydown where the chord needs one), then the action fires once; the table covers F2, F3, F5, F11, F12, Control+F5 and Shift+F10 (7 cases). (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "rename: F2")
- Given a store on document with an arrow chord registered, when the arrow key is dispatched with the right modifier flags, then the action fires once; the table covers Alt+ArrowUp, Alt+ArrowDown, Control+Shift+ArrowLeft, Control+Shift+ArrowRight, Control+ArrowUp and Control+ArrowDown (6 cases). (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "move-line-up: Alt+ArrowUp")
- Given a store on document with a punctuation chord registered, when the character is dispatched with its physical code and Ctrl held, then the action fires once; the table covers Control with "+", "-", "0", "/", "[", "]" and backtick (7 cases). - Given the sequence hotkey "g>g" and a keydown/keyup of g followed by a second keydown of g, when the second step lands, then the action fires once. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "VS Code: g>g (go to top - vim)")
- Given the sequence hotkeys "g>i" and "g>p", when g then the second letter is pressed, then each fires once. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "GitHub: g>i (go to issues)"; zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "GitHub: g>p (go to pull requests)")
- Given the modifier sequences "Control+k>Control+s" and "Control+k>Control+c", when each step's main key is dispatched with ctrlKey true (and no standalone Control keydown, which would be processed as a sequence step, fail to match and reset the sequence), then the action fires once. - Given both "Control+S" and "Control+Shift+S" registered on one store, when Ctrl+S is pressed then only save fires, and when Ctrl+Shift+S is pressed then only save-as fires and save is not re-fired. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "distinguishes Ctrl+S from Ctrl+Shift+S")
- Given both "/" and "Control+/" registered, when "/" alone is pressed then only the bare command fires, and when Ctrl+/ is pressed then only the Ctrl command fires. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "distinguishes single key from modified version")
- Given "Control+S" registered, when plain s is pressed with no modifier, then the action does not fire. (zag: packages/utilities/hotkeys/tests/smoke.test.ts: "Ctrl+S does not fire on plain S")
